I think you're missing my meaning. I'm not saying we need to psychoanalyze Sayo to understand the "true meaning" of the story, but how *we* become part of the story is important for what it means. If Sayo presents it to us, why? What does that say about Sayo, that she would give us this information? Why us? Why now? What does it say about *us* that she would let us into her world?
Conversely, if we are meant to be an omniscient observer of this world, and we only gain access to this information because that's how stories work, what does *that* say about Umineko? What does it mean if we have no place in this history? If we have no intrinsic ties to that world? If that world is, at the end of the day, accepting of its obvious status as purely fictional?

Content: EP 4 vague stuff ||I've heard that ep4 is a lot of backstory/buildup which is great cause im a sucker for these IF they matter later on||

The main issue is that the villains don't monologue about the themes enough, and the human characters barely get to flashback to all the people they're fighting for, because they're too busy throwing out endless meaningless jargon to describe their moves. This is why My Hero Academia smartly chooses to remove all tactics or high-concept abilities from the story in favour of every fight being decided by punching harder. Horikoshi doesn't bother to pretend that the winner of the fight is going to be decided by anything other than fiat, so he knows that coming up with setpieces is a waste of time. Instead, he uses the time to develop the emotional core of the conflict between the two characters. Umineko's fight scenes would benefit from a similar approach.

Content:
Ok, time to solve some muuuurddeeeeers! UMINEKO STREAM THEORIES:
||
I decided to ignore EVERY scene that Battler doesn't witness directly - none of these scenes receive meta-commentary from Battler and Beatrice, so they seem purely speculative to me.

I also ignore Episode 1 and analyze the Episode 2 in isolation.

The murder in the chapel:
- This is probably the most straightforward locked room without many gimmicks - one door and one key which wasn't accessible in the timeframe of the murder.
- Culprit probably used the gold to lure in the victims (or killed them beforehand, doesn't really matter)
- Due to Beatrice's reluctance to say certain red truths, someone had interacted with Maria's handbag, but NOT to access the key? Why? Plant some other envelope? Use her notebook? Steal some candy?
- The insistence on simplicity of this locked room leaves me with strong suspicion, which is very meta. It's the classic of locked room mysteries - the room that was never locked in the first place! I actually played another mystery game with such solution to locked room mystery last year, so it immediately came to my mind.
- Rosa was the one to "open" (or pretend to open) the chapel, and was REALLY insistent on demonstrating how the doors work. Intentionally or not, she also lead more people to witness the locked room.
||
